node.title: Re^3: Why does eof have a prototype?
node.author: haukex
node.doctext:
eof(); and eof; are (magically) different syntax for eof, and this difference can't be expressed with prototypes.

I'm not sure this is a job for prototypes. Every Perl function can be called with and without parens (given the compiler knows about it), it's always valid syntax. The trick would be to detect inside a hypothetical sub myeof whether the parens are there are not - how would one do this with prototypes? Seems more like a job for something like [doc://caller]. It's also worth noting that AFAIK [doc://eof] is the only function in Perl that behaves this way... the exception that confirms the rule ;-)

Interesting side note: see [doc://perltie#EOF-this|eof in perltie].

A "can be parsed without errors" criteria is not enough for me.

I don't think that's the criteria. It's more like: "Every variation of the builtin's syntax can be expressed by prototypes" - look at threads like [id://1207882] where everyone's implementations got close to the original, but noone was able to replicate all of [doc://sort]'s syntax. All of [doc://eof]'s syntax can be replicated, but not its functionality. That's where the difference is.

I do understand how you are interpreting that piece of documentation, but I think you should cut the authors some slack :-) [doc://eof] is a unique case, and knowing this, I don't think that passage is inaccurate.
